# Introduction

The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB) commissioned PolicyEngine
to estimate the effects of fifteen reforms to the taxation of Social Security
benefits over 2026-2100. They range from repealing the tax on benefits to taxing
all benefits, and they include senior-deduction and credit redesigns, two swaps of
that tax for income tax on employer payroll contributions, and a reverse-Roth
design. We also report a shorter phase-in of one swap as a sensitivity case. We
simulate every reform on the full populace microdata at a set of anchor years,
interpolate between them, and publish the annual results, trust-fund splits, and
household impacts on an
[interactive dashboard](https://policyengine.org/us/taxation-of-benefits-reforms).

## Current-law baseline

Under current law, beneficiaries pay income tax on part of their Social Security
benefits once their combined income (modified adjusted gross income, or MAGI,
plus half of benefits) exceeds statutory thresholds. They include up to 50
percent of benefits in taxable income above the first threshold and up to 85
percent above the second [@irs2024pub915]. The Treasury credits that revenue to
the Social Security Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) trust
funds and the Medicare Hospital Insurance (HI) trust fund [@ssa2026trustees;
@medicare2026trustees].

We score every reform against current law under the 2026 Trustees Reports'
intermediate assumptions. The Trustees built the 2025 reconciliation act (the
One Big Beautiful Bill Act) into those assumptions [@ssa2026trustees], including
the temporary bonus senior deduction, which expires after 2028 [@jct2025bonus].
PolicyEngine models the same law, so our simulations and our calibration targets
describe one current law. Several reforms extend, repeal, or replace the bonus
senior deduction, so its scheduled expiration shapes their effects.
